description: Meursault does not cry at his mother's funeral. In 123 pages of stripped-down prose, Camus invents the absurd.

hero.hook: “Maman died today.” One simple sentence. Then a trial about everything except the murder.

blocks.text: **The Stranger**, published in **1942**, was the first novel by **Albert Camus**. In **123 pages** of **blank writing**, a flat style with no ornament, it follows **Meursault**, an office clerk in Algiers whose indifference to social convention destroys him.

The book turns the **[[absurd in Camus]]** into fiction. The absurd is born from the clash between our hunger for meaning and the silence of the world. Meursault never fakes what he feels, and that refusal is exactly what condemns him.

**Albert Camus** grew up in the French Algeria of the 1930s, in a poor family marked by silence, and **[[Colonial Algeria as context]]** shapes the whole book. He built the cycle of the absurd out of three works: the novel **The Stranger**, the essay **The Myth of Sisyphus**, and the play **Caligula**.

blocks.caption: Albert Camus: clear sight, revolt, and a refusal to pretend

blocks.text: For Camus, the absurd does not end in nihilism, the belief that nothing means anything, but in **revolt**: living on without any higher meaning. The novel was published by **[[Gallimard]]**, a prestigious Paris house, in the middle of the **Occupation**, France under Nazi rule. Camus set out an ethic of clear sight in a world in crisis.

sections.title: Camus and the cycle of the absurd

blocks.text: Meursault refuses to lie about his feelings, at his mother's funeral and with **Marie**, his girlfriend. He lives by the present and by physical sensation, heat, light, tiredness, more than by the morality society imposes. His behavior shocks people because he will not play the part of the grieving son.

blocks.caption: The beach outside Algiers: crushing light, the trigger of the drama

blocks.text: In the Algerian French of the time, “maman” was an ordinary word of affection, without the childish ring it carried in mainland France.

Blinded by the sun on a beach, Meursault shoots an “Arab” the book never names. The act comes from neither hatred nor revenge, but from a tragic coincidence. That missing name has fed **[[postcolonial]]** readings, critical studies of colonization and of the way it pictured the people it ruled.

sections.title: Meursault: the man without a mask

blocks.text: The trial is not only about the murder. The prosecutor holds it against Meursault that he drank coffee with milk beside his mother's coffin and went to the movies the next day. Society condemns the man who refuses the shared rituals of mourning. The novel shows that public morality can punish harder than criminal law.
Maman died today. Or yesterday maybe, I don't know.

Meursault is sentenced to death for having “buried his mother with crime in his heart.” Facing the chaplain, he claims his life as his own and accepts the “gentle indifference of the world.” He finds a kind of peace in seeing clearly.

**Jean-Paul Sartre** explained why the clipped first-person style mattered so much. The novel points ahead to the **[[Nuveau Roman]]**, the movement of the 1950s that broke the conventions of storytelling. Critics working in **[[postcolonial]]** studies question the victim's anonymity, a silence filled by **[[Kamel Daoud]]**, an Algerian writer, in “The Meursault Investigation.”

events.detail: The Stranger is published by Gallimard.
events.title: Publication

events.detail: Meursault is judged on his feelings, not only on his crime.
events.title: A moral conviction

blocks.text: Camus is not writing a philosophy manual. He shows a man who refuses ready-made phrases, and who pays for it. Sun, beach, courtroom: every concrete detail builds toward a larger question about the meaning of life. The novel is still one of the most translated texts of the 20th century, read as much for its style as for its ideas.
**The Stranger** shows the **[[absurd in Camus]]**: Meursault is condemned less for his crime than for refusing to fake the emotions society demands.

sections.title: A shock that has not faded
